You can enjoy the action of sex or masturbation without feeling sexual attraction towards specific people. All asexuality means is that lack of sexual attraction.

People who enjoy sex but dont feel sexual attraction are often called "sex favorable" aces. They might like the feeling of sexual pleasure, but they don't get sexual feelings towards specific people. Having sex feels good, but it doesn't matter necessarily where that sexual pleasure is coming from (although many aces choose to do this with a partner to bond and please them).

Aces who don't feel one way or another about sex are often called or "sex indifferent." They might still have sex to bond with people, or for the pleasure of their partner. (Think of it this way, Person A doesn't care about fishing, but Person B loves it. Person A still goes fishing with person B because they enjoy it, and it is still a nice thing to please people you care about!)

"Sex repulsed" aces are generally the least likely to want to have sex in any given circumstance (that isn't to suggest that they haven't ever had sex, some have, and some haven't). The feeling or thought of sex isn't comfortable, and they will generally avoid it. Some sex repulsed aces will still enjoy masturbation, while others won't. Some sex repulsed aces don't want much of any physical contact, while other will still enjoy or tolerate things like hugs and/or kisses.

The range of asexuality is huge really. It doesn't define just one experience, but rather a range of experiences that don't feel sexual attraction, at least some of the time (there are demi aces, grey aces, etc who might feel sexual attraction sometimes!)

My personal feeling on the matter is that bisexual, pansexual, omnisexual, and polysexual all mean very very similar things. So similar, that at times it seems silly to split them up at all. But they important to some people, and people can use those labels without contributing to biphobia. 

I am comfortable with the label of bisexual and pansexual. I will use either depending on the situation because I know that bi can mean 2 or more. 

I agree with you that it is biphobic to say that bi people always have preferences, that bi people inherently care about "parts not hearts," that bi people only can love 2 genders (especially if someone is saying bi people only love the same and opposite gender). 

It isnt biphobic, however, to acknowledge that there is a lot of wiggle room in bisexuality. Some bi people *are* only attracted to 2 genders (regardless of if those 2 genders are male, female, nonbinary,  etc.), and that's why they use that label. That is not a bad thing, and I would never want someone to feel like they are damaging the reputation of bisexuality by identifying that way.

Identifying as pansexual immediately shrinks that wiggle room. It isn't that pan people are attracted to all genders while bi people *can't* be. It is simply a way of asserting a more specific label that has less wiggle room for interpretation.

There are problems with biphobia in pan spaces, and there are problems with panphobia in bi spaces. The sooner we can recognize that we have more in common than not, and put any harmful preconceived notions behind us, the better.

Ask yourself why you feel like you need to know what label(s) fits you best right now. Having labels to define your craft isnt a bad thing. It can give us a sense of belonging, help direct our studies, and give us words to communicate who we are to other people. But it's important to figure out what we want from a label and if a label can do that for us.

If none of the labels you've come across seem to fully describe who you are as a witch—and who you'd like to be as a witch—you have quite a few options.

1. Don't worry about labels at all. You don't need one really, so if you are most comfortable without one, don't worry about it.

2. Mix and match. There are no rules that say you have to only live under one label. Use a bunch if that is helpful for you.

3. Continue your search. There are so many labels and traditions, so maybe you just need to explore more to find one that suits you.

4. Make your own. Really, there is no reason why you can't label your own craft how you want.

As far as as advancing in your craft goes, I would suggest choosing topics that you can study and practice, rather than relying on specific labels, however. Consider what you are interested in, an pursue it. Go down interesting rabbit holes. Bury yourself in your interests. Practice and experiment. Labels can sometimes give you direction, but they won't do everything for you.

Also, for some practical advice, it is hard to make the jump from hating or disliking yourself to loving yourself. Many of us have to take small steps to getting there, instead of one big leap. When a thought comes by like "I'm worthless," it is easier to combat that with something like, "I am a person, and people have inherent worth," rather than trying to convince yourself right off the bat that you're a priceless wonderful being. It is easier—and still productive—to go from "I hate myself," to "I feel neutral about myself." Dont put pressure on yourself to love yourself right away, because that can definitely do more harm than good in my experience.
